{{Short description|Kind of arithmetic error}}
{{image frame|width=150|caption=Anomalous cancellation in [[calculus]]|border=no|content=<math>\begin{array}{l}
\;\;\; \dfrac     {d}      {dx} \dfrac{1}{x}
\\  =  \dfrac     {d}      {d}  \dfrac{1}{x^2}
\\  =  \dfrac{\cancel{d}}{\cancel{d}} \dfrac{1}{x^2}
\\  =  -                        \dfrac{1}{x^2}
\end{array}</math>}}
An '''anomalous cancellation''' or '''accidental cancellation''' is a particular kind of [[arithmetic]] procedural error that gives a numerically correct answer. An attempt is made to [[Reduction (mathematics)|reduce]] a [[fraction]] by cancelling individual [[Numerical digit|digit]]s in the [[numerator]] and [[denominator]]. This is not a legitimate operation, and does not in general give a correct answer, but in some rare cases the result is numerically the same as if a correct procedure had been applied.<ref>{{Mathworld|title=Anomalous Cancellation|urlname=AnomalousCancellation}}</ref> The trivial cases of cancelling trailing zeros or where all of the digits are equal are ignored.

Examples of anomalous cancellations which still produce the correct result include:

{{columns-list|colwidth=15em|
* <math>\frac{19}{95} = \frac{1\cancel{9}}{\cancel{9}5} = \frac{1}{5}</math>
* <math>\frac{16}{64} = \frac{1\cancel{6}}{\cancel{6}4} = \frac{1}{4}</math>
* <math>\frac{26}{65} = \frac{2\cancel{6}}{\cancel{6}5} = \frac{2}{5}</math>
* <math>\frac{49}{98} = \frac{4\cancel{9}}{\cancel{9}8} = \frac{4}{8} = \frac{1}{2}.</math><ref name=boas>[[Ralph P. Boas, Jr|Boas, R. P.]] "Anomalous Cancellation." Ch. 6 in ''Mathematical Plums'' (Ed. R. Honsberger). Washington, DC: [[Mathematical Association of America|Math. Assoc. Amer.]], pp.&nbsp;113&ndash;129, 1979.</ref>
}}

These and their inverses are all the cases in base 10 with the fraction different from 1 and with two digits. The article by [[Ralph P. Boas, Jr|Boas]] analyzes two-digit cases in [[radix|base]]s other than [[base 10]], e.g., {{sfrac|32|13}} = {{sfrac|2|1}} and its inverse are the only solutions in base 4 with two digits.<ref name=boas/>

An example of anomalous cancellation with more than two digits is {{sfrac|165|462}} = {{sfrac|15|42}}, and an example with different numbers of digits is {{sfrac|98|392}}={{sfrac|8|32}}.

==Elementary properties==

When the base is prime, no two-digit solutions exist.  This can be proven by contradiction: suppose a solution exists.  [[Without loss of generality]], we can say that this solution is

<math display="block">\frac{a||b}{c||a}=\frac{b}{c},\ {\rm base}\ p,</math>

where the double vertical line indicates [[Concatenation (mathematics)|digit concatenation]].  Thus, we have

<math display="block">\frac{ap+b}{cp+a}=\frac{b}{c}\implies (a-b)cp=b(a-c)</math>

But <math>p>a,b,a-c</math>, as they are digits in base <math>p</math>; yet <math>p</math> divides <math>b(a-c)</math>, which means that <math>a=c</math>.  Therefore. the right hand side is zero, which means the left hand side must also be zero, i.e., <math>a=b</math>, a contradiction by the definition of the problem.  (If <math>a=b</math>, the calculation becomes <math>\frac{a||a}{c||a}=\frac{a}{c} \implies \frac{a||a}{a||a}=\frac{a}{a}=1</math>, which is one of the excluded trivial cases.)

Another property is that the numbers of solutions in a base <math>n</math> is odd [[if and only if]] <math>n</math> is an even square.  This can be proven similarly to the above: suppose that we have a solution

<math display="block">\frac{a||b}{c||a}=\frac{b}{c}</math>

Then, doing the same manipulation, we get

<math display="block">\frac{an+b}{cn+a}=\frac{b}{c}\implies (a-b)cn=b(a-c)</math>

Suppose that <math>a>b,c</math>.  Then note that <math>a,b,c\to a,a-c,a-b</math> is also a solution to the equation.  This almost sets up an [[involution (mathematics)|involution]] from the set of solutions to itself.  But we can also substitute in to get <math>(a-b)^2n=b^2</math>, which only has solutions when <math>n</math> is a square.  Let <math>n=k^2</math>.  Taking square roots and rearranging yields <math>ak=(k+1)b</math>.  Since the [[greatest common divisor]] of <math>k,(k+1)</math> is one, we know that <math>a=(k+1)x,b=kx</math>.  Noting that <math>a,b<k^2</math>, this has precisely the solutions <math>x=1,2,3,\ldots,k-1</math>: i.e., it has an odd number of solutions when <math>n=k^2</math> is an even square.  The [[converse (logic)|converse]] of the statement may be proven by noting that these solutions all satisfy the initial requirements.

The question in a bit more generality was studied by Satvik Saha, Sohom Gupta, Sayan Dutta and Sourin Chatterjee.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Saha |first=Satvik |last2=Gupta |first2=Sohom |last3=Dutta |first3=Sayan |last4=Chatterjee |first4=Sourin |date=2024-01-01 |title=Characterising Solutions of Anomalous Cancellation |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12045-024-1737-2 |journal=Resonance |language=en |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=51–68 |doi=10.1007/s12045-024-1737-2 |issn=0973-712X|arxiv=2302.00479 }}</ref> The number of solutions in different bases are listed in [[oeis:A366412|OEIS A366412]].
